Global Industrial Machinery Corp. - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Global Industrial Machinery Corp., or GIMC, Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. If you would like to register for a question, please press star then one on your telephone keypad. If at any point your question has been answered and you would like to delete it from the queue, please press star then two. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss GIMC's results for the third quarter of 2024. Joining me on today's call are John Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; and Michael Chen, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to John Reynolds.

John Reynolds (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on GIMC's performance for the third quarter of 2024. We've made significant progress on several fronts, delivering a record backlog of $4.2 billion, up 15% year-over-year, fueled by robust bookings and operational execution. We've sharply reduced lead times across our key products and components, enhanced demand visibility in core end markets like construction, mining, agriculture, and manufacturing, accelerated growth in our automation and digital solutions, and continued to gain market share against key competitors. These achievements underscore our strategic focus on supply chain resilience, technical innovation, and customer-centric execution in the industrial equipment space.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Michael Chen to provide more detail on our financial results and operational deep dives.

Michael Chen (CFO):
Thank you, John. Turning to our financial performance, GIMC reported $2.75 billion in revenue for the third quarter, representing a 12% increase year-over-year. Gross margin expanded to 42%, driven by favorable product mix, pricing discipline, and efficiency gains from our Industry 4.0 investments. Operating expenses were $550 million, reflecting targeted investments in R&D and capacity expansion, resulting in an operating income of $680 million. Our net income for the quarter was $520 million, or $2.10 per diluted share.

We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet, with $1.5 billion in cash and cash equivalents. We are committed to investing in our business to drive future growth and shareholder value.

As we dive deeper into the operational metrics that underpin this record backlog of $4.2 billion—up 15% year-over-year—let's turn to lead times, a critical leading indicator for our manufacturing execution and customer satisfaction in the industrial equipment sector.

For those new to our story, lead times represent the elapsed duration from order acknowledgment to shipment readiness for our core portfolio, including heavy earthmoving equipment like our flagship GIMC-450 hydraulic excavators, precision CNC machining centers under the Apex line, and mission-critical components such as high-torque servo motors, forged steel gearboxes, and programmable logic controllers, or PLCs. These metrics are tracked via our SAP S/4HANA ERP system, segmented by product family, region, and supply tier.

Starting with the headline: our weighted average lead time across key products and components has improved to 16.2 weeks as of quarter end, down 22% sequentially from 20.8 weeks in Q2 and a robust 28% year-over-year from 22.5 weeks in Q3 2023. This marks our best quarterly performance since pre-pandemic levels in 2019, when averages hovered around 14 weeks. Capacity utilization at our primary facilities in Peoria, Illinois, and Monterrey, Mexico, now sits at 92%, up from 85% a year ago, reflecting disciplined capital allocation from our $450 million CapEx program.

Breaking it down by product category: In the heavy equipment segment, which is 45% of backlog, lead times for excavators and wheel loaders have compressed to 18 weeks from 24 weeks year-over-year, driven by a 35% ramp in weld hall throughput at our expanded Ohio facility. Book-to-bill remains strong at 1.4x, with backlog visibility extending 32 weeks. Comparatively, peers like Caterpillar reported similar pressures easing to 20 weeks in their latest print, but our vertical integration in chassis fabrication gives us a 2-3 week edge.

In automation and precision tools, 30% of backlog, CNC centers and robotic arms are at 14 weeks, a 15% quarter-over-quarter improvement, thanks to our adoption of digital twin technology via Autodesk Fusion 360 simulations, which cut prototyping cycles by 40%. This segment benefits from softer semiconductor constraints—global chip lead times, per the SIA index, fell to 18 weeks from 26 weeks last year.

For key components, 25% of backlog, we've made outsized gains. Servo motors and PLCs are now at 10 weeks, down 30% year-over-year, after diversifying away from single-source Asian suppliers amid ongoing U.S.-China tariffs. Gearbox forgings, heavily reliant on specialty alloy steel, improved to 12 weeks from 19 weeks, supported by our new just-in-time partnership with Nucor in the U.S. Midwest. Notably, electronic component lead times dropped 25% sequentially due to forward contracts with TSMC equivalents and our strategic inventory build of $120 million in Q2, now yielding a 4-week buffer.

Regionally, performance varies meaningfully, underscoring our nearshore-first strategy amid global fragmentation. In North America, 60% of revenue, lead times average 15 weeks, bolstered by reshoring tailwinds from the CHIPS Act and IIJA infrastructure spend. Our Monterrey plant's proximity to U.S. customers has captured 12% market share gains in mining equipment, outpacing Deere's industrial segment.

In EMEA, 25% of revenue, at 19 weeks, slightly extended due to energy volatility—Russian gas curtailments inflated European steel premiums by 18% year-over-year per Platts indices—but mitigated by our new Duisburg, Germany, assembly line, which localized 70% of components and trimmed intra-regional delays.

Asia-Pacific, 15% of revenue, lead times here remain challenged at 22 weeks, pressured by typhoon-related disruptions in Taiwan and softening demand in China’s property sector. However, our joint venture with Komatsu in Japan has stabilized bulldozer deliveries, with a 10% quarter-over-quarter improvement.

What’s driving these trends? First, supply chain resilience: We've reduced supplier concentration from 40% single-source exposure in 2022 to under 15% today, via RFx processes and AI-powered forecasting with IBM Watson, which improved demand signal accuracy by 25% and curbed excess inventory by $80 million.

Second, technical initiatives: Our $50 million investment in Industry 4.0—including Rockwell Automation's FactoryTalk platform and Siemens NX for CAM optimization—has boosted throughput 18% without proportional headcount growth. We're also piloting additive manufacturing for gearbox prototypes at our R&D center in Austin, targeting a 50% lead time reduction for custom spares by FY25.

Strategically, these shorter lead times are a competitive moat in an industry where customers like Rio Tinto or Vulcan Materials prioritize uptime over price. We've seen conversion rates on RFQs rise 22% as we quote sub-20-week deliveries versus competitors' 25+ weeks. Pricing power has followed: average selling prices up 8% year-over-year, with no dilution from discounting. Looking forward, we guide Q4 averages to 15.5 weeks, assuming no major port strikes or raw material shocks—steel scrap indices are stable at $380/ton.

In summary, lead time compression validates our operational playbook and positions us to harvest backlog into FY25 with margins expanding 200 basis points to 22%.

Now, turning to demand trends across our core end markets—construction, mining, agriculture, and manufacturing—which collectively represent about 85% of our backlog and continue to drive our record $28.5 billion order intake in Q3. Overall, we saw a 7% year-over-year increase in bookings, with visibility extending 14 months out, supported by healthy aftermarket growth at 12% and parts utilization rates above 95% across our dealer network.

Starting with construction, which accounts for 35% of our equipment revenue, demand remains resilient, up 9% year-to-date on a constant-currency basis. This is fueled by unprecedented infrastructure spending globally. In North America, U.S. housing starts held steady at 1.35 million annualized units, but non-residential activity—particularly data centers—has been the standout, with hyperscalers like Amazon Web Services and Microsoft committing over $200 billion in capex this year alone. We've seen our large excavator and telehandler orders surge 18%, akin to the boom Caterpillar highlighted in their recent quarters.

Regionally, Europe is mixed: U.K. and German infrastructure projects under the EU's €800 billion NextGenerationEU fund are offsetting residential softness, but high interest rates have pushed pipeline conversion rates down to 65% from 75% last year. Asia-Pacific, led by India's $1.4 trillion National Infrastructure Pipeline, delivered 15% order growth for our compact track loaders and wheel loaders, where we've gained share through our Tier 4 Final compliant engines.

On the technical front, we're accelerating electrification: our 50-ton battery-electric excavator prototype, co-developed with ABB, is in field trials at a U.S. data center site, targeting 20% lower OPEX via regenerative braking and fast-charging. Strategically, we're prioritizing backlog allocation to high-margin segments like autonomous dozers—our MineStar-inspired system has reduced cycle times by 15% in demos—while managing inventory destocking in rental fleets, where utilization dipped to 72% industry-wide per IronPlanet data.

Mining, representing 25% of our mix, is our brightest spot, with bookings up 14% year-over-year and a $12 billion backlog—the highest in our history. Copper prices hovering at $4.50 per pound, driven by EV and renewable demand, have spurred greenfield projects, while iron ore stability above $100/tonne supports ultra-class haul trucks. We've booked 45 new 400-tonne rigid-frame trucks this quarter, comparable to Komatsu's strong PC8000 sales.

Latin America shines brightest: Chile and Peru account for 60% of our mining orders, with Codelco's expansion adding 2 million tonnes of annual copper capacity, boosting demand for our high-altitude optimized drills. Australia remains steady at 8% growth, buoyed by Rio Tinto's autonomous fleet expansions, where our Command for Hauling tech integrates seamlessly, delivering 10-12% productivity lifts. North America saw a slight pullback to 5% growth due to labor constraints, but ESG pressures are accelerating adoption of our waterless dust suppression systems.

Technically, we're at the forefront of autonomy and sustainability: our 793F electric-drive trucks, with 25% lower fuel burn via e-axle tech, are in production ramp, and we've launched a hydrogen-fuel-cell retrofit kit for legacy loaders, piloted with BHP. Strategically, we're expanding capacity at our Peoria facility by 20% for OEM drivetrains, targeting 15% market share in battery-electric underground equipment by 2026, while hedging commodity exposure through long-term offtake agreements with OEMs like Epiroc.

Agriculture, at 20% of revenue, grew 4% in bookings, navigating headwinds from softening farm incomes—U.S. net farm income projected at $128 billion by USDA, down 5% year-over-year—yet buoyed by a multi-year replacement cycle for aging fleets averaging 12 years old. High-horsepower tractors over 200 HP saw 12% demand uplift, mirroring Deere's trends, driven by precision ag upgrades.

North America led with 7% growth: corn and soy yields at record 182 and 52 bushels/acre supported sprayer and planter orders, where our AutoTrac guidance systems boast 99.9% uptime. Brazil's sugarcane ethanol boom added 10% to combines, but China weakened 8% due to oversupply and stimulus delays. Europe faces headwinds from Ukraine supply disruptions and EU Green Deal subsidies favoring smaller, electric tractors—our 50-100 HP segment grew 6% there.

Initiatives include our NextSwath tech for end-row turns, reducing overlaps by 12% and fuel use by 8%, now standard on 70% of new tractors. We're scaling electric orchard sprayers with John Deere-inspired battery packs, targeting 30% emissions cuts for compliance with California's CARB rules. Strategically, we're reshoring ag implement production to Mexico via our new Ramos Arizpe plant, cutting lead times 25%, and bundling telematics subscriptions—our JD Link equivalent—at 85% attach rates for recurring revenue.

Rounding out with manufacturing at 25% of our portfolio, demand rose 6%, propelled by onshoring and factory automation. U.S. CHIPS Act and IRA investments—$52 billion and $370 billion respectively—have ignited semiconductor and battery gigafactory builds, spiking material handler orders 11%. Mexico's nearshoring wave, with auto OEMs like Tesla and BMW expanding, drove 20% growth in our Latin American forklift backlog.

EMEA industrial capex rebounded 5%, led by German machine tools, while Asia-Pacific softened 2% amid China's property woes but held firm in semiconductors via TSMC's U.S. fabs. Our Raymond electric pallet trucks saw 15% uptake, competing with Crown Equipment on narrow-aisle efficiency.

Key initiatives: IoT-enabled predictive maintenance via our Vital Insights platform flags 95% of failures pre-downtime, integrated with Siemens MindSphere. We've rolled out collaborative robots for weld cells, boosting throughput 18%. Strategically, we're acquiring a stake in a modular skid steer OEM to enter the EV supply chain, with capacity for 50,000 units annually, and focusing 40% of R&D on Industry 4.0 digital twins for 10-15% yield improvements.

In summary, end-market demand is constructive, with mining and construction providing tailwinds, ag steady, and manufacturing gaining steam—positioning us for 8-10% organic growth in FY24. Risks include geopolitical tensions in LatAm and potential Fed pauses, but our 42% gross margins, $4.2 billion liquidity, and dealer inventory at 7 months' supply give us flexibility. Strategically, we're doubling down on electrification—15% of 2024 capex—autonomy, targeting 20% of mining fleet sales, and services, aiming for 35% of revenue by 2026. We'll continue share gains through innovation, as evidenced by our 250 basis points market share expansion per AEM data.

Before moving on, I'd like to highlight one of our brightest growth stories: the rapid expansion of our automation and digital offerings, and their profound impact on operational efficiency for both our customers and our business model. As you know, GIMC is a leader in industrial equipment for heavy manufacturing—think CNC machining centers, robotic welding systems, and precision assembly lines—and we've been at the forefront of Industry 4.0 since our launch of the AutoLink IIoT Suite back in 2019.

The numbers speak volumes. Our Automation and Digital segment delivered exceptional results this quarter, posting 28% year-over-year revenue growth to $1.2 billion, representing 22% of total company revenue—up from just 14% a year ago. Hardware automation sales, including our next-gen RoboForge collaborative robots and adaptive servo systems, grew 18% year-over-year to $650 million. But the real standout is our digital offerings—software, analytics, and subscription services—which surged 42% to $550 million, with annual recurring revenue now at $720 million, up 35% year-over-year and boasting a net retention rate of 118%. This shift toward high-margin, sticky SaaS revenue is transforming our P&L: segment EBITDA margins expanded 450 basis points to 32%, driven by 85% gross margins on digital services versus 45% on traditional hardware.

This growth isn't happening in a vacuum; it's fueled by secular tailwinds in the manufacturing sector. The global industrial automation market is projected to hit $350 billion by 2028, per McKinsey, with a 12% CAGR, accelerated by labor shortages—U.S. manufacturing alone faces a 2.1 million worker gap by 2030, according to Deloitte—and the push for reshoring amid geopolitical tensions. Our customers, from automotive giants like Ford and Volkswagen to aerospace leaders like Boeing, are deploying automation to boost throughput amid these pressures.

Now, on impact to efficiency, which is the core value proposition. Our digital offerings, powered by the AutoLink platform—our edge-to-cloud IIoT ecosystem—are delivering measurable ROI for clients. Predictive maintenance, using AI-driven anomaly detection on vibration, thermal, and acoustic data from our sensors, has reduced unplanned downtime by an average of 35% across our installed base of 150,000+ connected assets. For instance, a major Tier-1 auto supplier in the Midwest integrated our Digital Twin module with their stamping lines, achieving a 22% uplift in Overall Equipment Effectiveness from 78% to 95%, while cutting energy consumption 18% via real-time optimization algorithms.

Regionally, North America, 45% of segment sales, grew 32% year-over-year, propelled by the CHIPS Act and IRA incentives driving semiconductor and EV battery fab builds. A key win was our $150 million contract with a Texas-based hyperscaler for automation in wafer fab equipment, where our ML-based process control reduced defect rates by 40%. Europe, 30% of sales, grew 25% despite softer macro, thanks to reshoring—German Mittelstand firms adopted our RoboForge systems en masse, with digital uptake at 65% attachment rates. Asia-Pacific, 20% of sales, accelerated 22%, led by China's 'Made in China 2025' into high-mix/low-volume electronics; we're navigating U.S. export controls by localizing edge computing in Singapore and Vietnam.

Strategically, R&D spend in this segment rose 15% year-over-year to $180 million, focusing on generative AI integration—partnering with NVIDIA to embed Jetson Orin modules for on-device federated learning, enabling zero-latency defect detection without cloud dependency. We've also rolled out 'AutoLink Sustainability Suite,' which uses digital twins to simulate carbon footprints, helping customers meet EU CBAM tariffs; early adopters like a Swedish steel mill saw Scope 1 emissions drop 12% while maintaining 98% uptime.

On the M&A front, our acquisition of Predictive Dynamics last year is paying dividends: their physics-informed neural networks have boosted our prescriptive analytics accuracy to 92%, contributing $80 million in cross-sell revenue this quarter. Looking ahead, we see digital services scaling to 40% of segment revenue by 2026, with churn under 5% due to outcome-based pricing—tying fees to OEE gains.

Finally, on market share dynamics across key end-markets, which continues to reflect the strength of our differentiated portfolio in precision machining centers, automated assembly systems, and heavy-duty material handling equipment. We track our share rigorously using independent data from sources like Gardner Intelligence and the Association for Manufacturing Technology, benchmarked against peers such as Haas Automation, DMG Mori, and Fanuc. Overall, we gained 120 basis points of global market share year-over-year in Q3, reaching 14.2% in our core CNC and robotics segments, up from 13.1% a year ago. This marks our third consecutive quarter of expansion, driven by organic wins, strategic pricing discipline, and our push into high-growth adjacencies like semiconductor fab equipment and EV battery production lines.

In North America, 42% of our revenue and our fortress, we captured 2.1 points of share in the automotive sector, growing from 16.5% to 18.6%. This was fueled by major wins at OEMs like Ford and GM for our next-gen FlexArm robotic welders, which integrate proprietary AI-driven adaptive control software—reducing cycle times by 22% and scrap rates by 15% compared to legacy Fanuc systems. In aerospace, we saw a modest 0.8-point erosion to 12.4% share, primarily due to Boeing's supply chain disruptions delaying orders for our TitanForge 5-axis mills. That said, our backlog in aerospace surged 28% quarter-over-quarter to $1.2 billion, signaling a rebound as RTX and Spirit AeroSystems ramp up 737 MAX and F-35 production.

In Europe, 28% of revenue, we navigated energy transition headwinds effectively. In oil & gas, we lost 1.2 points to 11.8% share amid Shell and TotalEnergies' capex cuts, but offset this with 3.4-point gains in renewables, hitting 17.2% in wind turbine nacelle assembly lines. Our EuroFlow hydraulic pump series, with 30% higher efficiency under the new EU Ecodesign Directive, secured €450 million in frame agreements with Vestas and Siemens Gamesa. Germany and the Nordics were standouts, with 85% utilization in our Dortmund facility supporting reshoring under the EU Chips Act.

Asia-Pacific, our highest-growth region at 22% of revenue, delivered outsized gains—up 4.7 points overall to 13.9% share. China was the engine, expanding from 9.2% to 14.1% in semiconductor equipment, displacing local players like Shenyang Machine Tool with our QuantumEdge etchers optimized for 3nm node fabs. TSMC's Arizona expansion is pulling through demand, but we're vigilant on U.S. export controls. In India, our market share in construction equipment doubled to 8.5%, thanks to partnerships with Larsen & Toubro for our MegaHaul autonomous dump trucks, which boast 25% lower TCO versus Caterpillar's 793F amid the $1.4 trillion National Infrastructure Pipeline.

Latin America and other emerging markets, 8% of revenue, saw flat-to-up performance, with Brazil's mining sector yielding a 2.3-point gain to 15.7% via Vale's adoption of our OreCrusher high-pressure grinders, which cut energy use by 18% in line with ESG mandates.

Strategically, these dynamics underscore technical leadership through our $250 million FY24 R&D capex, including 15% to digital twins and cobot integrations for Industry 4.0; capacity optimization, with greenfield expansions in Mexico and Vietnam boosting output 20% without diluting margins—our adjusted EBITDA margin held at 22.4%; and customer intimacy, evidenced by 92% renewal rate on service contracts for IoT-enabled predictive maintenance, generating $180 million in recurring ARR.

Looking forward, we expect 100-150 basis points of annual share gains, targeting 16% global share by FY26, assuming stable macro. Risks include steel tariffs inflating BOM costs 5-7% and potential softening in China capex to 4% from 7%. But with a $4.8 billion backlog—up 19% year-over-year—and win rates at 42% versus peers' 35%, we're well-positioned.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then one. Our first question comes from Ben Smith with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Ben Smith (JPMorgan):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the demand environment you're seeing in the mining market?

John Reynolds (CEO):
Good morning, Ben. Thanks for the question. Mining continues to be a standout for us, as Michael outlined, with 14% year-over-year booking growth and that historic $12 billion backlog. Copper at $4.50 per pound is driving greenfield expansions, particularly in Latin America where Chile and Peru make up 60% of our orders—Codelco's ramp is a prime example, pulling in our high-altitude drills. Australia's steady 8% growth ties to Rio Tinto's autonomous fleets, where our Command for Hauling delivers 10-12% productivity gains. Even with North America's 5% pullback from labor issues, ESG is accelerating our waterless systems. Our electric-drive 793F trucks and hydrogen retrofits position us for the supercycle, and we're expanding Peoria capacity 20% for drivetrains. Visibility is strong out 14 months, and we see this tailwind persisting into FY25.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Chen with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen (Goldman Sachs):
What are your expectations for capital expenditures in the coming year?

Michael Chen (CFO):
Thanks, Lisa. Our FY24 CapEx came in at $450 million, focused on capacity and resilience, like the Ohio weld hall and Monterrey expansions that drove our lead time compression. For FY25, we're guiding to $500-550 million, a 10-20% increase, with 15% earmarked for electrification—like scaling the ABB-co-developed battery excavators and hydrogen kits—and another 20% for Industry 4.0 digital twins and AI forecasting. This includes $50 million more for additive manufacturing pilots and edge computing localization in APAC. Returns are clear: we've hit 92% utilization, throughput up 18%, and ROIC above 25% on recent projects. This supports 8-10% organic growth while keeping free cash flow at $800 million-plus. No major shifts unless macro accelerates reshoring further.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Lee (Morgan Stanley):
How are you managing supply chain disruptions, and what impact are they having on your margins?

John Reynolds (CEO):
David, great question, and one that ties directly to our lead time progress. We've transformed our supply chain, cutting single-source exposure from 40% to under 15% through RFx and IBM Watson AI forecasting—demand accuracy up 25%, excess inventory down $80 million. Our $120 million strategic buffer and Nucor JIT for forgings got components to 10-12 weeks, even with EMEA steel premiums up 18% from energy issues. Regional strategies like nearshoring in Monterrey captured 12% mining share gains. Margins benefited: gross at 42%, up from pricing power—ASPs +8%—and efficiencies like FactoryTalk boosting throughput 18%. Disruptions like Taiwan typhoons linger in APAC at 22 weeks, but our Komatsu JV improved that 10% QoQ. Net impact is positive—200 bps margin expansion guided for FY25—as shorter leads convert RFQs 22% better. We're resilient and gaining ground.

Operator:
There are no further questions at this time.

John Reynolds (CEO):
Thank you for your questions and your interest in GIMC. We are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Sarah Thompson (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call. Have a great day.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
